articleTitle: Some telephone switching problems
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper attempts to analyse and explain in an elementary manner the problems involved in inter-connecting the various subscribers in a single telephone area, both manually and automatically. Technical terms are defined, the apparatus used in both cases is briefly described, and the inherent advantages of the automatic system are illustrated by analysis and comparison of the operations and signals involved in an isolated exchange. Automatic operation of larger and of multi-exchange areas is explained by a similar process of comparison, and the automatic devices used are then described in more detail, the essential desiderata being discussed.

articleTitle: Notes on commutators
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Commutator and brush gear troubles may be broadly classified as being due to either electrical or mechanical causes. The introduction of commutating poles as a fundamental feature in the design of continuous current machines, and the control of commutation, and knowledge of its limitations thereby obtained, have resulted in the elimination of many of those old troubles; which were due primarily to defective electrical conditions of commutation. A further check on these conditions is afforded by the stringent tests now applied to every machine before issue to service, and it is safe to say that nowadays troubles arising from inherent bad commutation are very rare. It is found, on the other hand, that the majority of apparent electrical troubles are traceable to mechanical defects.

I am of the opinion that no application of electricity to the needs of mankind has received such an impetus through the war as that relating to medicine and surgery.

abstract: (Associate Member): I agree with Capt. McArthur that to obtain reliability excess strength is quite unnecessary, but the statement be criticises did not advocate excess of any kind. On this question I cannot do better than quote the following statement made by Mr. F. R. McBerty, who was associated with the development of automatic telephony from the beginning: — “In designing this apparatus it was in mind that the apparatus must be made in electrical factories as they exist, and the equipment must be taken care of by maintenance men in telephone exchanges as they exist. An automatic telephone exchange switch can be built perhaps as small as a watch, but it is hardly conceivable that we could maintain such a piece of apparatus as that. Therefore, this system has been designed on the same lines as the central battery system, namely, sufficiently substantial and rigid and non-adjustable to put into the hands of men who would be found in ordinary circumstances to maintain it, to stand a fair chance of working properly and requiring little attention. Having put in heavy and rigid portions, such as might be required for long service, it followed as practically necessary that it must be driven to power.” (Post Office Institution of Electrical Engineers, London, Discussion on Mr. B. O. Anson's paper: “The Western Electric Company's Automatic Telephone System.”)

articleTitle: Fondation george montefiore
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A notification has been received from the “Association des Ingénieurs électriciens sortis de l'Iustitut électrotechnique Montefiore, of Liége, giving the conditions governing the competition for the 1917 Fondation George Montefiore, which, owing to the war, has been held over for decision in 1921. The award is made every three years following an international competition for the best original work submitted on the scientific advancement and on the progress of the technical applications of electricity in all its branches, excluding popular works or those of mere compilation. The papers must have been written within the three years preceding the closing date of the competition. They should be drawn up either in French or English, and may be printed or typewritten. Twelve copies of the work presented must be sent. Works may be submitted anonymously, but such works should bear a device, which must be repeated on the outside of a sealed packet attached to the matter. The packet must contain the full Christian names and surname of the author, together with his signature and full address, legibly written.

articleTitle: Automatic telephony
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate Member): I feel we must all congratulate Messrs. Parsons and Griffith on their exceedingly instructive paper, which is one of the very few on the subject of Telephony which has been read before this Institute since its inauguration. The enthusiastic reception it has met with indicates that the time has passed when our friends, the power and lighting engineers, looked on the telephone man as one who came into your office with a wooden box tinder his arm and left nothing but a mess of disfigured plaster and bad language in his wake. The authors have, I think, shown us that there is some thing more in the art of telephony than this. I regret, however, that they have confined themselves to descriptions of cir cuits and apparatus and have left out the discussion of such problems as to why the automatic system should be adopted in any given area on an economic basis : taking into account the question of first cost, depre ciation, maintenance, labour and operating efficiency as compared with the manual system. Further, I should like them to have dealt with the interesting subject of the efficiency of junction groups. I hope, however, that the present is only the first of further papers which the authors will give us on Automatic Telephony. A paper of this kind obviously entails an enormous amount of work on the authors, and I must congratulate them on their success in putting before us so clearly the essential parts of the highly complicated circuits involved in the two systems described. As representative of one of the companies concerned in the manufacture of the Systems described in the paper, it would be out of place for me to attempt any comparison of their merits. I should like, however, to clear up a few misapprehensions regarding the Western Electric System which have appeared during the discussion. First of all I think that the distinction between direct and revertive control has not been fully realised.

articleTitle: Notes on small suction gas plants
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member): I have read Mr. Newsham's contribution in the Institute's Transactions on the subject of Small Suction Gas Plants. His description of the process of gas making will be of interest to those who have not had the opportunity of studying this side of engineering science, although, I suppose those will be few and far between these days. The author's classifications are, if I may say so, somewhat loose and probably misleading. He talks of and describes what he terms the older type of plant, and compares this with what he terms the gas plant of to-day, which, he says, is virtually fool proof. He may be able to judge what is fool proof better than I can, but I venture to say that the gas plant has not yet been made which could in any sense be described as fool proof. It is true that a skilled mechanic is not required to run them, but even the unskilled worker or native who can ran a suction gas plant cannot be described as a fool. If he can be so described, he will quickly demonstrate how many opportunities the present day suction plant affords him for the exercise of his folly. The expression earlier types of plant and the gas plant of to-day convey nothing to us. I believe certain makers claim that their plants ten years ago embodied features which are still in use and which have been recently copied by others. In these cases the earlier type is the plant of to-day. Presumably the author has one particular make of plant in view and doubtless the present type of this make is a great improvement on its predecessors, but that does not justify his generalisation on the subject. I gather that his principal claim for his present day type of plant is that it is built on what has been called the open-hearth principle, but open-hearth plants have been in use in this and other countries for twelve years at least, and their introduction was practically synonymous with the practical development of the suction gas producer. Earlier types of plant, therefore, include the open-hearth tpye and most of the troubles experienced by the author in his earlier types were not and could not be experienced by those who had the foresight fifteen years ago to make a plant that the author has apparently only discovered.

abstract: In Mr. Baynes' reply to the discussion of this paper an error occurred in the printed account (see page 200 of the October, 1920, issue, Vol. XI., Part 10). In discussing two-rate meters having their rate changed by a lowering of the voltage at the time desired, be mentions a method by which the time-switch introduces resistance into the armature circuit during the periods of the low rate.
